title: Is the Economy Booming, or Just Growing?

narration.licence: commercial: Azure AI Speech terms allow the generated audio in published media

sentences.text: The American economy grew in both quarters of 2026 we have numbers for, and yet by September the average hourly paycheck bought less than it had a year before.
So is this a boom, or are workers going backwards?
Which side is right depends on which number you look at.
Donald Trump has put one side plainly: "The economy is the greatest economy we've ever had by far."

sentences.text: Start with the boom: how fast is the economy actually growing?
Real GDP, the value of everything the country produces after stripping out price rises, grew at an annual rate of 2.5 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and 2.2 percent in the second.

chart.note: Annualised quarterly rates; the third quarter is not yet published.

sentences.text: That is solid growth, but Federal Reserve officials put the economy's long-run pace at 2.0 percent a year, so this runs only a little above normal, not the surge the word boom suggests.

chart.title: Growth against the long-run pace
chart.note: The long-run figure is the median FOMC projection, not a measurement.

sentences.text: What about jobs?
The unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in September, and it has stayed between 4.1 and 4.3 percent since March.
At its September press conference, the Federal Reserve's chair said "the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment".

onScreenText: "the unemployment rate is basically running consistent with full employment"

citations.label: Federal Reserve chair, press conference, 16 September 2026
citations.detail: Federal Reserve: "FOMC Press Conference, September 16, 2026" youtube.com/watch?v=ELU3u2Ny7r0

sentences.text: But payrolls barely moved: employers added just 29,000 jobs in September.
And the jobs report itself never defines full employment, so calling this full employment is a judgement, not a measurement.
Now the paycheck, the number most people actually feel.
In the year to January 2026, pay beat prices, and average hourly earnings after inflation were up 1.2 percent.

sentences.text: One limit: these are averages across all employees, so they cannot tell you how the worker in the middle of the pay scale did.

So is the economy booming? By these measures, no: it is growing a little faster than the Fed's long-run pace, with unemployment right at the level Fed officials expect it to settle at, but slow hiring.
Growth and shrinking real pay are not a contradiction: in 2026 they ran side by side, because output, jobs and what a paycheck buys are different measurements.
So the next time someone tells you the economy is booming, or that it is broken, ask one question: which number?
